chunks: A number of our companions narrated from Sahl ibn Ziyad from Ja'far ibn Muhammad al-Ash'ari from Ibn al-Qaddah from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

A man challenged a certain person from Banu Hashim to a duel (al-baraz), but he refused to duel him. The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) asked him, 'What prevented you from dueling him?' He replied, 'He was the horseman (strongman) of the Arabs, and I feared that he would overpower me.' The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him and his family) said to him, 'Indeed, he has transgressed against you. If you had duelled him, you would have overcome him. And if a mountain transgresses against a mountain, the transgressor is crushed.'

And Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'Indeed, al-Husayn ibn Ali (peace be upon them both) challenged a man to a duel. The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) learned of this and said, 'If you do something like this again, I will reprimand you. And if someone challenges you to something like this and you do not respond, I will also reprimand you. Have you not noticed that it is transgression (bagh)?'
ai.seo_question: What is the Shia ruling on accepting or refusing a duel (baraz) based on the concept of transgression (bagh)?
ai.summary: This narration from al-Kafi elucidates the jurisprudential nuance of 'al-baraz' (single combat) by distinguishing between mere fear of defeat and the specific condition of 'bagh' (transgression/aggression) by the challenger. It records Imam al-Sadiq’s dual instruction to both initiate and accept duels, while Ali ibn Abi Talib’s response to a Banu Hashim member illustrates that even a renowned warrior like 'Fars of the Arabs' is not exempt from combat if the challenge constitutes aggression. This highlights the Shia scholarly view that courage is obligatory when facing unjust aggression, regardless of the opponent's perceived strength.
